records.citation: Pelland JC, et al. The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains. Sports Med. 2026;56(2):481-505.
records.population: Healthy adults in 67 resistance-training studies; participants were predominantly young and male.
records.limitations: Meta-regression is observational across studies, indirect-set counting remains model-dependent, and the sample was 79% male with a mean age near 25 years. It does not define an individual optimum.

records.citation: Mcleod JC, et al. The influence of resistance exercise training prescription variables on skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function in healthy adults: An umbrella review. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(1):47-60.
records.population: Healthy adults represented in 44 systematic reviews of resistance-training prescription variables.
records.limitations: An umbrella review inherits overlap and limitations from included reviews. Evidence was sparse for physical function and insufficient for several isolated variables.

records.citation: Moesgaard L, et al. Effects of Periodization on Strength and Muscle Hypertrophy in Volume-Equated Resistance Training Programs: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2022;52(7):1647-1666.
records.population: Healthy trained and untrained adults in volume-equated resistance-training interventions.
records.limitations: Benefits were clearer for 1RM strength, especially in trained participants; hypertrophy did not differ when volume was equated. Few studies supported comparisons beyond linear and undulating models.

records.citation: Singer A, et al. Give it a rest: a systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on the effect of inter-set rest interval duration on muscle hypertrophy. Front Sports Act Living. 2024;6:1429789.
records.population: Healthy adults in nine randomized resistance-training studies comparing inter-set rest durations.
records.limitations: Only nine studies with heterogeneous protocols were included. Estimates overlapped substantially and do not establish one best rest interval for every exercise or goal.

records.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, et al. Effect of repetition duration during resistance training on muscle hypertrophy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2015;45(4):577-585.
records.population: Healthy people in eight resistance-training studies lasting at least six weeks.
records.limitations: Only eight studies qualified, most sets were taken to failure, and very slow repetitions were poorly studied. Tempo cannot be reduced to a universal hypertrophy code.

records.citation: Jukic I, et al. The Acute and Chronic Effects of Implementing Velocity Loss Thresholds During Resistance Training: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Evaluation. Sports Med. 2023;53(1):177-214.
records.population: Mostly trained adults in velocity-loss resistance-training studies.
records.limitations: Exercise, load and training history modify the response; much of the evidence concerns trained men and device-measured bar velocity. Thresholds are not interchangeable across exercises.

records.citation: Hickmott LM, et al. The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med Open. 2022;8(1):9.
records.population: Resistance-trained people in 15 studies of load or volume autoregulation.
records.limitations: The evidence base was small and heterogeneous, with no clear overall 1RM advantage for autoregulated versus percentage-based loading. Findings do not validate app-only automatic load changes.

records.citation: Orange ST, et al. Comparison of velocity-based vs traditional resistance training methods on strength, power, and sprint speed: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and quality appraisal. J Sports Sci. 2022;40(11):1220-1234.
records.population: Apparently healthy participants in four randomized trials comparing velocity feedback with traditional resistance training.
records.limitations: Only four trials and 88 participants were available; evidence quality was low to very low and estimates were imprecise.

records.citation: Silva Oliveira P, et al. Comparison of Polarized Versus Other Types of Endurance Training Intensity Distribution on Athletes' Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2024;54(8):2071-2095.
records.population: Adult and young-adult endurance athletes in 17 intervention studies.
records.limitations: A small VO2peak advantage was concentrated in short interventions and highly trained athletes; time trial and other outcomes were similar. Protocols and zone definitions varied.

records.citation: Rosenblat MA, et al. Which Training Intensity Distribution Intervention Will Produce the Greatest Improvements in VO2max and Time-Trial Performance in Endurance Athletes? Sports Med. 2025;55(3):655-673.
records.population: Recreational and competitive endurance athletes in 13 studies with 348 individual participants.
records.limitations: Only studies comparing polarized training were eligible, women were underrepresented, and results differed by performance level. No model was universally superior.

records.citation: Wang Z, et al. Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One. 2023;18(5):e0282838.
records.population: Endurance athletes in 14 tapering studies.
records.limitations: Studies were few and heterogeneous, many subgroup estimates were based on small samples, and athlete-specific competition schedules limit generalization.

records.citation: Bourdon PC, et al. Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2017;12(Suppl 2):S2-161-S2-170.
records.population: Athletes and practitioners using internal and external training-load monitoring.
records.limitations: Consensus concepts do not validate one metric, threshold, or injury-prediction model. Athlete monitoring practice is not automatically transferable to recreational users.

records.citation: Kellmann M, et al. Recovery and Performance in Sport: Consensus Statement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018;13(2):240-245.
records.population: Athletes and practitioners considering training stress, fatigue and recovery.
records.limitations: Consensus provides a framework rather than a validated recovery score; responses vary within and between people and no single marker captures recovery.

records.citation: Meeusen R, et al. Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of ECSS and ACSM. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2013;45(1):186-205.
records.population: Athletes with possible functional overreaching, nonfunctional overreaching or overtraining syndrome.
records.limitations: Overtraining syndrome is a clinical exclusion diagnosis with no single accepted marker. SportRX cannot diagnose it from RPE, completion or performance trends.

records.citation: Ingram LA, et al. Optimising the Dose of Static Stretching to Improve Flexibility: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Multivariate Meta-regression. Sports Med. 2025;55(3):597-617.
records.population: Adults in 189 acute or chronic static-stretching studies.
records.limitations: Meta-regression describes group averages and flexibility outcomes, not pain treatment, safe end range, or a personalized stretching dose.

records.citation: Konrad A, et al. Chronic effects of stretching on range of motion with consideration of potential moderating variables: a systematic review with meta-analysis. J Sport Health Sci. 2024;13(2):186-194.
records.population: Healthy participants represented in 77 chronic stretching studies.
records.limitations: Substantial heterogeneity was present and flexibility gains do not imply injury prevention, pain reduction, or improved sport performance.

records.citation: Oxfeldt M, et al. Effects of plyometric training on jumping, sprint performance, and lower body muscle strength in healthy adults: a systematic review and meta-analyses. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2019;29(10):1453-1465.
records.population: Healthy recreationally active adults and athletes in 25 lower-body plyometric studies.
records.limitations: Interventions lasted 4-12 weeks and sprint and strength estimates were heterogeneous. The review does not establish beginner readiness or a safe landing progression.

records.citation: Milanovic Z, et al. Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2015;45(10):1469-1481.
records.population: Healthy adults aged 18-45 years in 28 controlled endurance-training studies.
records.limitations: The synthesis used magnitude-based inferences, protocols varied, and results in young healthy adults do not establish safety or superiority for every user.

records.citation: Poon ETC, et al. Interval training versus moderate-intensity continuous training for cardiorespiratory fitness improvements in middle-aged and older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sports Sci. 2021;39(17):1996-2005.
records.population: Middle-aged and older adults in 14 interval or continuous training studies.
records.limitations: Only 14 studies with 429 participants were included and interventions were short. Findings do not bypass preparticipation screening or individual tolerance assessment.

records.citation: Spiering BA, et al. Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time. J Strength Cond Res. 2021;35(5):1449-1458.
records.population: General, athletic and military populations discussed in a narrative review of reduced training dose.
records.limitations: This is a narrative review with limited direct evidence, especially for athletes and older adults. Maintenance estimates must not be treated as universal minima or improvement doses.
